subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on the periodic table, then mark my answer against the CCEA spec.
promptWeak: Explain the periodic table for GCSE CCEA Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing:
questions.explain: The modern periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number (number of protons).

questions.q: A horizontal row in the periodic table is called a:
questions.explain: Horizontal rows are periods; vertical columns are groups.

questions.q: Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have:
options: The same number of electrons in their outer shell
questions.explain: Chemical properties depend on outer electrons, and all elements in a group have the same number of outer-shell electrons.

questions.q: An element has electronic configuration 2,8,2. Which period and group is it in?
questions.explain: Three occupied shells means period 3; two outer electrons means Group 2.

questions.q: Where are most non-metals found in the periodic table?
questions.explain: Non-metals are found towards the right-hand side; metals are on the left and centre.

questions.q: How many electrons do all Group 1 elements have in their outer shell?
questions.explain: Group 1 (alkali metals) all have 1 electron in their outer shell, which they lose to form 1+ ions.

questions.q: What is produced when a Group 1 metal reacts with water?
options: A metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas
questions.explain: Alkali metals react with water to form a metal hydroxide (an alkaline solution) and hydrogen gas, e.g. 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2.

questions.q: As you go down Group 1, reactivity:
questions.explain: Reactivity increases down Group 1: the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.

questions.q: Why is potassium more reactive than sodium?
options: Its outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily
It has more protons in the shell
questions.explain: Potassium's outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is more shielded, so it is lost more easily, making it more reactive.

questions.q: How many electrons do Group 7 (halogen) atoms have in their outer shell?
questions.explain: Halogens have 7 outer electrons and gain 1 electron (or share) to form 1- ions with a full outer shell.

questions.q: At room temperature, what is the state and colour of chlorine?
questions.explain: Chlorine is a green/yellow gas. Bromine is an orange/brown liquid and iodine is a grey/black solid at room temperature.

questions.q: As you go down Group 7, reactivity:
questions.explain: Reactivity decreases down Group 7: the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so it is harder to attract and gain an electron.

options: Bromine displaces chlorine from sodium chloride
Iodine displaces chlorine from sodium chloride
Iodine displaces bromine from sodium bromide
Chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide
questions.explain: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one. Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from sodium bromide.

questions.q: What is the ionic equation product colour change when chlorine is added to potassium iodide solution?
options: Solution turns brown as iodine is displaced
questions.explain: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces iodine: Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2. The iodine formed turns the solution brown.

questions.q: Why are the Group 0 noble gases very unreactive?
options: They have a full (stable) outer shell of electrons
questions.explain: Noble gases have a full outer shell, so they have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons, making them very unreactive (inert).
Because they are unreactive and do not need to bond, noble gases exist as individual (monatomic) atoms.

questions.q: Which is a typical property of transition metals compared with Group 1 metals?
questions.explain: Transition metals typically form coloured compounds, have high melting points and densities, and are often used as catalysts, unlike the more reactive Group 1 metals.
Transition metals and their compounds are commonly used as catalysts, e.g. iron in the Haber process.

questions.q: A feature of transition metals is that they can form ions with:
options: More than one oxidation state (variable valency)
questions.explain: Transition metals often form ions with different charges (variable oxidation states), e.g. iron forms Fe2+ and Fe3+.
